question: What findings should make me raise a cholera alert (suspected outbreak) in my area, and how quickly does it have to be reported?
reference: A cholera alert is: (A) two or more people aged 2 years or older with acute watery diarrhea and severe dehydration, or dying from acute watery diarrhea, from the same area within 1 week of one another; or (B) one case of acute watery diarrhea testing positive for cholera by RDT in an area that has not yet detected a confirmed case. It must be reported to the surveillance focal point or person in charge immediately (within 30 minutes).
quote: Two or more people aged 2 years or older with acute watery diarrhea and severe dehydration, or dying from acute watery diarrhea, from the same area within 1 week of one another

question: A 7-year-old with cholera has stopped vomiting. Which antibiotic should I give, at what dose, and what can I use instead if that drug isn't suitable?
reference: For children under 12 years the first-line antibiotic is doxycycline 2–4 mg/kg orally as a single dose. Alternatives are azithromycin 20 mg/kg (max 1 g) or ciprofloxacin 20 mg/kg (max 1 g) orally as a single dose. Antibiotics are given once the patient can take oral medication (vomiting has stopped).
quote: Children < 12 years old Doxycycline 2-4 mg/ kg p.o. single dose Azithromycin 20 mg/kg (max 1g) p.o. single dose, or ciprofloxacin 20 mg/kg (max 1g) p.o. single dose

question: A 3-year-old comes to the CTC severely dehydrated from cholera. How should I give the IV Ringer's lactate — how much and over what time?
reference: For patients 1 year old and above, give 30 ml/kg IV in the first 30 minutes, then 70 ml/kg IV over 2½ hours (100 ml/kg Ringer's Lactate in total). (Infants under 1 year: 30 ml/kg over 1 hour, then 70 ml/kg over 5 hours.)
quote: Age First give 30ml/kg IV in Then give 70ml/kg IV in Infants (<1year) 1 hour 5 hours 1year old and above 30 minutes 2 ½ hours

question: For a reactive oral cholera vaccination campaign with the stockpile vaccines, how far apart should the two doses be given, and from what age can people be vaccinated?
reference: Shanchol and Euvichol-Plus are each given as a two-dose regimen, with the doses a minimum of 14 days apart. The recommended age for vaccination is 1 year or older.
quote: Shanchol™ and Euvichol-Plus® are each recommended to be given as a two-dose regimen, with the two doses given a minimum of 14 days apart. The recommended age for vaccination is 1 year or older.

question: Our emergency nutrition survey found an acute malnutrition rate of 12% with no aggravating factors. Which food and nutrition interventions do the surveillance benchmarks call for?
reference: For an acute malnutrition rate of 10–14% (or 5–9% with aggravating factors): no general rations, targeted supplementary feeding, and therapeutic feeding of severely malnourished individuals.
quote: Acute malnutrition rate 10 -14% OR 5%-9% with aggravating factors* No general rations Targeted supplementary feeding Therapeutic feeding of severely malnourished

question: In an emergency vitamin A supplementation round, what preventive dose and how often should infants aged 6–12 months and children over 1 year receive?
reference: Infants 6–12 months: 100,000 IU orally every 4–6 months. Children over 1 year: 200,000 IU orally every 4–6 months.
quote: Infants 6-12 months 100,000 IU Every 4-6 months Children > 1 year 200,000 IU Every 4-6 months*

question: If a displaced population is relying completely on general food distribution, what is the minimum energy the ration has to provide per person?
reference: The rations must provide at least 2,100 kcal per person per day.
quote: If the population is entirely depending on general food rations as a source of food, then the rations must provide at least 2100 kcal per person per day

question: Which diseases are prioritized for climate-sensitive disease surveillance in Ethiopia?
reference: Dengue fever, malaria, yellow fever, cholera and meningococcal meningitis.
quote: Climate sensitive diseases prioritized under climate sensitive disease surveillance in Ethiopia are Dengue fever, Malaria, Yellow fever, Cholera and Meningococcal Meningitis.

question: How long does the malaria parasite need to develop inside the mosquito at about 25 °C, and below what temperatures does this development fail to complete?
reference: At 25 °C sporogony takes 12–14 days for P. falciparum and slightly less (11–12 days) for P. vivax; it takes longer at lower temperatures. Sporogony does not complete below 19 °C for P. falciparum and below 16 °C for the other species.
quote: At a temperature of 25 °C, 12 – 14 days are required for P. falciparum (or about 4 feeding cycles). Slightly less for P. vivax (11 – 12 days), at lower temperatures, Sporogony takes longer time. Below 19 °C for P. falciparum, and 16 °C and for the other species Sporogony does not complete.

question: In the climate-sensitive disease case definitions, when should a patient be classified as a suspected case of meningococcal meningitis?
reference: Any person with sudden onset of fever (>38.5 °C rectal or 38.0 °C axillary) and one of the following signs: neck stiffness, altered consciousness, or other meningeal signs such as bulging fontanel or convulsion.
quote: Any person with sudden onset of fever (>38.5 °C rectal or 38.0 °C axillary) and one of the following signs: neck stiffness, altered consciousness, or other meningeal signs such as bulging fontanel, convulsion

question: Under community and event-based surveillance, how many households is one CEBS focal person expected to look after?
reference: There is one CEBS focal person per WDA/HDA, which means one focal person manages up to 30 households (or according to the local community structures).
quote: meaning that one CEBS focal person will manage up to 30 households or based on local implementation of community structures

question: What signs in a newborn should make a health extension worker suspect neonatal tetanus?
reference: Any newborn with a normal ability to suck and cry during the first two days of life who, between the 3rd and 28th day of age, cannot suck normally and becomes stiff or has convulsions or both.
quote: Any newborn with a normal ability to suck and cry during the first two days of life, and who, between the 3rd and 28th day of age, cannot suck normally, and becomes stiff or has convulsions or both.

question: Besides the listed priority diseases, what other kinds of events must be notified immediately under CEBS?
reference: Unusual and unknown occurrences of diseases and/or conditions; clusters of cases and/or deaths of humans and animals that may indicate public health hazards; and rumors of unexplained deaths of humans and animals.
quote: Unusual and unknown occurrence of diseases or/and conditions  Cluster of cases and/or death of humans and animals that may indicate p ublic health hazards  Rumors of unexplained death of humans and animals

question: At kebele level, who is the technical coordinator of CEBS, and where and how often should community notifications be reported onward?
reference: The health extension worker (HEW) is the technical coordinator of CEBS at kebele level. The HEW receives rumor notifications from CEBS focal persons and should document and report community notifications to the catchment health center on an immediate and/or weekly basis.
quote: The HEW should document and report community notifications to the catchment health center on immedi ately and/or weekly basis.

question: A child in the outpatient therapeutic programme still hasn't met the cure criteria. After how long is she classed as a non-responder, and when would a child instead be counted as a defaulter?
reference: Non-responder: does not reach the SAM discharge criteria after 16 weeks (4 months) in treatment. Defaulted: absent for two consecutive visits (default should be confirmed).
quote: Defaulted Absent for two consecutive visits. Default should be confirmed. Non-responder Does not reach the SAM discharge criteria after 16 weeks (4 months) in treatment.

question: Which routine antibiotic should a child with severe acute malnutrition but no medical complications receive, at what dose and for how long?
reference: Oral amoxicillin 25 mg/kg every 12 hours for 5 days (or until referral to OTP).
quote: NO MEDICAL COMPLICATIONS Amoxicillin oral: 25 mg/kg every 12 hours for 5 days or until referral to OTP

question: When screening in the community, what MUAC cut-offs classify moderate acute malnutrition in pregnant or lactating women and in people aged 60 years or older?
reference: With no bilateral pitting oedema and no medical complications, MAM is MUAC < 23.0 cm for pregnant and lactating women, and MUAC 18.5 to 21.0 cm for older people aged 60 years or more.
quote: MAM No bilateral pitting oedema. No medical complications* Children 6-59 months: MUAC ≥11 .5 to <12.5 cm or WFH ≥-3 to <-2 z scores PLW: MUAC < 23.0 cm Older people≥60 years: MUAC 18.5 to 21 .0 cm

question: What isoniazid dose should I prescribe for TB preventive therapy in adults and in children, for how long, and should anything be given with it?
reference: INH 300 mg/day for adults and 10 mg/kg for children, given daily for six months. Vitamin B6 (25 mg/day) is advised alongside isoniazid to prevent INH-induced peripheral neuropathy.
quote: The dose of INH is 300mg/day for adults and 10mg/kg for children daily administered for six months. It is also advised to co-administered vitamin B-6 (25mg/day) with Isoniazid to prevent INH-induced peripheral neuropathy

question: For drug-susceptible TB, when do I record a treatment outcome as 'treatment failure' versus 'lost to follow-up'?
reference: Treatment failure: sputum smear or culture positive at month 5 or later during treatment. Lost to follow-up: a patient who has been on treatment for at least four weeks and whose treatment was interrupted for eight or more consecutive weeks.

question: Within what time must a leprosy patient finish their MDT doses to be recorded as 'treatment completed', for paucibacillary and for multibacillary leprosy?
reference: PB: six monthly doses completed within nine months. MB: twelve monthly doses completed within 15 months.
quote: Treatment completed: A patient who has completed a full course of MDT within the prescribed period (six months doses in nine months for PB, and twelve months doses in 15 months for MB).
